text: Your own SQL Server instance, sitting on your own network, simply isn't reachable directly from the Power BI service running out in the cloud. The on-premises data gateway is the piece of software that actually bridges that gap for you.

Requests come in from the cloud service, the gateway relays them securely to your local SQL Server behind the scenes, and nothing on your own network ever gets exposed directly to the public internet in the process. This is exactly the missing piece behind that SQL Server connector setup all the way back in Chapter 2 — you needed a gateway, or a live Desktop session, to make that connection actually work at all.

Three distinct gateway types exist, each fitting a different situation. Standard is fully shareable across multiple users and multiple data sources, the right choice for any real team setup. Personal mode is solo, Power BI only, and simply can't be shared with anyone else at all. Virtual network needs no local installation whatsoever, fully managed instead by Microsoft directly.

Five real steps put a gateway to actual use. Download and install it on a machine that can genuinely reach your SQL Server. Configure it properly for your firewall and network requirements. Add gateway admins who can help manage it going forward. Use it to actually refresh a real on-premises data source. And troubleshoot whatever issues inevitably come up along the way.

Every single lab in this entire course that connects to AdventureWorks or Northwind through the SQL Server connector depends completely on this gateway existing and staying online. Lesson 77 covers scheduling that refresh properly, once the gateway itself is confirmed up and running.
